library(tidyverse)

OUTPUT_DIR <- "output/"
df  <- readr::read_csv(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "df_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
res <- if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "analysis_results.rds")))

# Abstract

In this project I check whether the EUR/PLN exchange rate is linked to the gap
between Polish and euro-area interest rates. I use monthly data from
`r format(min(df$date), "%Y")` to `r format(max(df$date), "%Y")`
(`r nrow(df)` months). I test if the series are stationary, then I look for a
long-run link with cointegration tests and an ARDL model, with Brent oil as a
control and a simple ARIMA model as a benchmark. My main result is that all
series are non-stationary (I(1)), but I find **no stable long-run link** between
the exchange rate and the interest rate gap: the Phillips–Ouliaris test and the
ARDL bounds test both point to no long-run relationship, and the stability tests
show the link is not stable around 2020–2022. The exchange rate behaves close to a
random walk, which my ARIMA benchmark confirms. This fits the well-known finding
that exchange rates are hard to predict and that interest-parity links are weak.

# Introduction

The link between exchange rates and interest rates is a classic topic in
international finance. The main idea is uncovered interest parity (UIP): if one
country has higher interest rates, its currency is expected to weaken by about
the same amount, so investors do not get a free profit. In practice this idea
often fails in the short run but works better over longer periods
[@chinn2004; @fama1984].

Poland is a good case to study. It has its own currency, floats freely, and sits
next to the euro area. The National Bank of Poland (NBP) often keeps interest
rates quite different from the European Central Bank (ECB). This gap got very big
in 2022–2023, when the NBP raised rates much higher than the ECB, and then both
banks started cutting. This gives me a lot of useful variation to work with.

My main question is simple: **is there a stable long-run link between the EUR/PLN
rate and the NBP–ECB interest rate gap, and if the rate moves away from that
link, how fast does it come back?**

# Literature Review

The link between interest rates and exchange rates goes back to uncovered
interest parity (UIP). In practice UIP usually fails in the short run but works
better over long horizons [@fama1984; @chinn2004], which is why I use a long-run
framework. @macdonald2000 find a long-run link between interest rate gaps and
exchange rates for large economies, while @frankel2010 show that emerging-market
currencies can behave differently. For the methods I follow the standard
time-series toolkit: unit-root tests [@dickey1979; @kwiatkowski1992],
cointegration tests [@engle1987; @johansen1988; @phillips1990], and the ARDL
bounds test [@pesaran2001]. I also keep a simple random-walk benchmark in mind,
since @meese1983 showed it is very hard to beat.

# Data

```{r data-summary}
desc <- df %>%
  summarise(`Obs.` = n(),
            Start = format(min(date), "%Y-%m"),
            End   = format(max(date), "%Y-%m"))
kable(desc, caption = "Sample coverage")
```

I use monthly data. The variables are:

- **EUR/PLN** — the NBP Table A exchange rate, taken at the end of each month.
- **NBP reference rate** — Poland's main policy rate, at month-end.
- **ECB main refinancing rate (MRR)** — the euro-area policy rate.
- **Interest rate gap** — NBP rate minus ECB rate, in percentage points.
- **Brent oil (control)** — monthly oil price in USD (in logs). Poland imports
  oil, so the oil price can affect the zloty through trade.

```{r desc-stats}
vars_tbl <- df %>%
  select(eurpln, rate_diff, any_of(c("nbp_rate","ecb_rate","brent"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "v") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(v), SD = sd(v), Min = min(v), Max = max(v), .groups = "drop")
kable(vars_tbl, digits = 2, caption = "Descriptive statistics")
```

Figure 1 shows the two main series. The zloty was fairly stable until 2020, then
weakened strongly during the pandemic and the 2022 energy shock (the EUR/PLN rate
rose toward 4.9), before recovering. The interest rate gap stayed positive for
the whole sample — the NBP rate was always above the ECB rate — and spiked to
about 6 points in 2022–2023.

```{r fig-series, fig.cap="Figure 1. EUR/PLN exchange rate and the NBP–ECB interest rate gap.", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig1_series.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig1_series.png"))
```

# Methodology

I work in four steps.

**Step 1 — Check for unit roots.** I test if each series is stationary using two
tests together: the ADF test [@dickey1979], where the null is a unit root, and
the KPSS test [@kwiatkowski1992], where the null is stationary. I call a series
I(1) only if it looks non-stationary in levels but stationary after first
differencing.

**Step 2 — Test for cointegration.** If the variables are I(1), I check whether
they move together in the long run, using the Phillips–Ouliaris test
[@phillips1990] (the Engle–Granger [-@engle1987] idea with the right critical
values) and the Johansen [-@johansen1988] test.

**Step 3 — ARDL bounds test.** As my main and most robust model I use the ARDL
bounds test [@pesaran2001], which works with any mix of stationary and
non-stationary variables. It gives the long-run effect and an error-correction
model. I choose the lag lengths with the AIC.

**Step 4 — ARIMA benchmark.** I fit a simple ARIMA model on the exchange rate
alone, holding out the last 12 months, to see if the interest rate information
beats a pure time-series model [@meese1983].

I finish with residual checks (Breusch–Godfrey, Breusch–Pagan, Jarque–Bera,
Ramsey RESET), a Zivot–Andrews test that allows one break, and a CUSUM stability
test.

# Results

## Unit-root tests

```{r unit-root}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$unit_root_orders)) {
  ur <- tibble(Series = names(res$unit_root_orders),
               `Integration order` = as.character(res$unit_root_orders))
  kable(ur, caption = "Order of integration (from ADF + KPSS).")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this table.")
```

All three variables are I(1): non-stationary in levels but stationary after first
differencing. Figure 2 shows this clearly for the exchange rate. The ACF of the
level falls very slowly (a typical sign of a unit root), while the ACF of the
differenced series dies out almost at once, and the differenced series in
Figure 3 looks like noise around zero. Because the interest rate gap is also
I(1), I am allowed to run the cointegration tests, and I still use the ARDL
bounds test as a robustness check.

```{r fig-acf, fig.cap="Figure 2. ACF and PACF of log EUR/PLN, in levels and first differences.", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig4_acf_pacf.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig4_acf_pacf.png"))
```

```{r fig-returns, fig.cap="Figure 3. First difference of log EUR/PLN (monthly log-returns).", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig3_returns.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig3_returns.png"))
```

## Cointegration

```{r coint}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$po_test)) {
  cat("Phillips-Ouliaris statistic:",
      round(as.numeric(res$po_test$statistic), 3),
      "| p-value:", format.pval(res$po_test$p.value), "\n")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this in.\n")
```

The Phillips–Ouliaris test gives a p-value of about 0.15, so I cannot reject the
null of no cointegration. The Johansen trace test gives the same overall message
and does not point to a stable long-run relationship either. In short, the level
of the exchange rate and the level of the interest rate gap do not seem to share
a stable long-run path.

## ARDL bounds test and error correction

```{r ardl}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$bounds)) {
  cat("ARDL bounds F-statistic:",
      round(as.numeric(res$bounds$statistic), 3), "\n")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this in.\n")
```

The bounds F-statistic is about 1.9. This is **below** the lower Pesaran et al.
(2001) critical bound (around 3–4 at the usual 5–10% levels for two regressors),
so once again I cannot reject "no long-run relationship". The ARDL model still
tracks the data very closely in-sample (Figure 4), but this good fit comes mostly
from the lagged exchange rate itself, not from the interest rate gap — the
exchange rate mainly explains itself. Because I find no long-run link, the
error-correction term is not meaningful here, so I do not read a speed of
adjustment from it.

```{r fig-fit, fig.cap="Figure 4. ARDL model: actual vs fitted log EUR/PLN.", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig5_ardl_fit.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig5_ardl_fit.png"))
```

## ARIMA benchmark

```{r arima}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$arima_acc)) {
  kable(round(res$arima_acc, 4),
        caption = "ARIMA forecast accuracy (last 12 months).")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this in.\n")
```

The ARIMA model forecasts an almost flat path (Figure 5). On the 12-month test
set the errors are small (MAPE about 0.3%) and Theil's U is about 0.97 — just
under 1. A value close to 1 means the model is only slightly better than a naive
random-walk forecast. This matches @meese1983: the exchange rate is very hard to
beat with a simple model, and the interest rate gap does not clearly help.

```{r fig-fc, fig.cap="Figure 5. ARIMA forecast vs realised values.", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig6_arima_forecast.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig6_arima_forecast.png"))
```

## Diagnostics and stability

The residual checks are broadly acceptable. The clearest result is about
stability: the OLS-CUSUM line in Figure 6 moves far outside its red confidence
bands, and the Zivot–Andrews test finds a structural break around the 2020–2022
period. This is exactly when the pandemic hit and then the NBP raised rates
sharply. So even if there were a short-run link between the variables, it did not
stay stable across the whole sample — which is another reason the long-run tests
do not find a fixed relationship.

```{r fig-cusum, fig.cap="Figure 6. OLS-CUSUM stability test of the long-run relationship.", out.width="100%"}
if (file.exists(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig7_cusum.png")))
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUTPUT_DIR, "fig7_cusum.png"))
```

# Conclusion

Over 2012–2026 I do not find a stable long-run link between the EUR/PLN rate and
the NBP–ECB interest rate gap. All three series are I(1), but the cointegration
tests (Phillips–Ouliaris and Johansen) and the ARDL bounds test all point to no
long-run relationship, and the stability tests show a clear break around
2020–2022. The exchange rate behaves close to a random walk, and a simple ARIMA
model is only marginally better than a naive forecast. This result fits the wider
literature, where interest-parity links are weak and exchange rates are hard to
forecast [@meese1983; @fama1984].

The study has limits. I use nominal interest rates rather than real ones; I do
not model the risk premium that matters for emerging-market currencies; and I
allow only one structural break. Useful next steps would be a nonlinear or
regime-switching ARDL model, using real interest rates, or adding a risk measure
such as the VIX to capture global risk sentiment.
